# **Chapter 1** **INTRODUCTION**

Oral health remains a persistent and measurable public health challenge among Filipino school children. The Department of Health's 2021 National Monitoring and Epidemiological Dental Survey reported that 92% of Filipinos have dental caries, with 78% of 12-year-old children affected and an average Decayed, Missing, and Filled Teeth (DMFT) score of 4.48, exceeding the World Health Organization's standard of 3 DMFT \[1\],  \[2\]. In response, the DOH has identified oral health as one of the eight priority areas under the National Objectives for Health Philippines 2023–2028 and has mandated school dental clinics to provide regular screenings and preventive treatments such as bi-annual fluoride varnish application through its School Dental Health Care Program \[3\], \[4\].  
Despite this mandate, school dental clinics, including those in Barangay Tanyag, Taguig City, continue to rely on manual, paper-based processes for managing student records, scheduling appointments, and generating reports. These practices introduce significant inefficiencies and the resulting fragmentation of data limits the clinics' ability to monitor student oral health trends, ensure follow-up care, and make timely, informed clinical decisions.  
Prior studies have demonstrated that electronic health records in dental practice can significantly reduce missing information and improve coordination among healthcare providers \[5\], \[6\]. Research has further shown that predictive analytics applied to dental records can support early intervention by identifying students at higher risk of developing oral health conditions and enabling more proactive treatment planning \[7\], \[8\], \[9\]. However, a gap persists between these demonstrated capabilities and actual implementation in resource-constrained, barangay-level school dental settings, where processes remain largely manual and fragmented.  
This study addresses that gap by proposing the design and development of Floral, a Dental Health Record Management System that centralizes student dental and treatment records across schools, enhances appointment management, and supports data-driven decision-making through automated reporting, with integrated predictive analytics in Barangay Tanyag, Taguig City to identify potential dental health risks and facilitate preventive dental care planning among students.   
**Background of the Study**  
Among the most common health problems affecting Filipino school children today is tooth decay, or dental caries. A national survey conducted by the Department of Health (DOH) in 2021 revealed that 92% of Filipinos have dental caries, with 78% of children aged 12 affected, and 49% already experiencing dentinogenic infection, a condition where tooth decay has progressed deep enough to affect the inner tissues of the tooth \[1\]. To measure the extent of tooth decay in a population, the World Health Organization (WHO) uses the Decayed, Missing, and Filled Teeth (DMFT) score as a standard. Filipino children aged 12 and below average a DMFT score of 4.48, which exceeds the WHO's acceptable benchmark of 3 DMFT \[2\]. Due to the high prevalence of dental caries among school children, oral health has been identified as one of the eight priority health areas in the National Objectives for Health (NOH) Philippines 2023–2028 by the DOH \[3\]. In line with this, the DOH issued guidelines for the implementation of the School Dental Health Care Program \[4\], which pushes school clinics to provide medical, dental, and nursing services. This includes the deployment of dentists on a rotational basis to conduct regular oral health screenings and provide necessary treatments.  
The urgency to address dental health challenges in school settings is further reinforced by its alignment with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Most directly, the SDG 3: Good Health and Well-Being, which seeks to ensure health and well-being for all, at every stage of life, addressing major health priorities including access to quality and affordable healthcare services. Improving access to dental care for school children through a digitized and efficient system directly contributes to this goal \[10\]. The study also aligns with SDG 4: Quality Education, which recognizes that good health is a prerequisite for effective learning. Children who suffer from untreated tooth decay often experience pain and discomfort that can affect their attendance, concentration, and overall academic performance \[11\]. By addressing dental health needs in school settings, the system supports conditions that allow students to learn better. It also connects to SDG 10: Reduced Inequalities, as greater efforts are needed to invest more in health and social protection, especially for young people and other vulnerable communities, and that reducing inequality requires ensuring equal opportunity and inclusive social growth \[12\]. By improving public dental services for students in a barangay-level community who may have limited access to private dental care, the system helps ensure that quality dental healthcare is not exclusive to those who can afford it. On an institutional level, the study aligns with SDG 16: Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions, particularly Target 16.6, which calls for developing effective, accountable, and transparent institutions at all levels \[13\]. It should promote data-driven, transparent, and accountable management of a government-mandated public health program through structured recordkeeping, automated reporting, and an audit trail. Together, these goals highlight that improving school dental health record management is not only a local necessity but also a contribution to broader national and global health and development commitments.  
Bridging these global commitments to the local level, however, reveals a contrast between policy intent and operational reality. School dental clinics, which serve as a primary setting for the early detection, prevention, and treatment of dental health issues among students, continue to operate under manual, paper-based systems that undermine the very goals these programs seek to achieve. Rather than functioning as efficient, data-driven points of care, many of these clinics remain burdened by outdated practices that limit their capacity to deliver consistent, quality dental services to the students who need them most. These methods make it difficult to efficiently track patient information and often lead to issues such as incomplete or disorganized records. In the current setup of school dental clinics in Barangay Tanyag in Taguig City, student records such as consent forms, oral histories, and dental charts are maintained only on paper, making them vulnerable to loss or damage. Manual dental charting can also be slow and prone to errors. Inconsistent handwriting and manual record updates may lead to misinterpretation of treatment records and delays in patient management. In addition, scheduling and communication with parents are handled through paper forms, phone calls, or text messages. Furthermore, the preparation of reports on the number of treated students and performed procedures is done manually, making data compilation time-consuming and prone to inaccuracies. Moreover, while students are mandated to receive dental services twice a year, the clinic struggles to systematically monitor and complete these required visits. The existing workforce consists of only one dentist and one dental aide handling three school dental clinics. Bagong Tanyag Integrated School, which serves as the dentist’s main clinic, accommodates students from kindergarten to Grade 10, while the other two schools, namely South Daanghari Elementary School and Bagong Tanyag Elementary School, cover kindergarten to Grade 6\. Each year level has over eight sections, with each section comprising approximately 45 students. In total, the clinics are responsible for managing around 8,000 student records. The clinic provides a range of dental services, including cleaning, filling, extraction, fluoride varnish, pit and fissure sealant, and silver diamine fluoride. The sheer volume of students, combined with limited personnel and persistent reliance on manual processes, further aggregates inefficiencies in record tracking, service delivery, and compliance with the twice-yearly mandate.  
As a result, there is an increasing need to adopt digital health solutions, such as electronic health records (EHRs), to improve data management and service delivery in school dental clinics, which the DOH has also encouraged as part of its NOH agenda \[3\]. This shift toward digitization is no longer optional but a necessary step in modernizing school dental care delivery. In addition, a study concluded that EHRs in dental practice significantly enhance clinical efficiency. The results confirmed that digital records can reduce the risk of missing information and improve coordination among healthcare professionals \[5\], \[6\]. Beyond digital record management, the integration of predictive analytics in healthcare systems has shown strong potential in supporting data-driven decision-making. Predictive models can be used to identify students who are at higher risk of developing dental health issues, prioritize treatment needs, and assist in planning preventive interventions such as fluoride application, which is particularly beneficial in school dental clinics where resources and time are limited. Studies have shown that predictive analytics using dental records can support treatment planning and early intervention, with models demonstrating strong capability in predicting untreated dental caries and enabling earlier scheduling of treatments. Other studies further highlight the value of timely dental monitoring, achieving high prediction accuracy for individual preventive care measures. Moreover, integrating predictive analytics into a dental health record management system extends its functionality beyond basic record-keeping by identifying and prioritizing high-risk patients based on existing data, thereby supporting efficient dental care delivery \[7\], \[8\], \[9\]. Despite this, a gap still exists between these technological advancements and their actual implementation in school dental clinics, where processes remain manual and technologies are not yet fully utilized.  
To address the challenges, this study proposes the development of a dental health record management system integrated with predictive analytics. The system is designed to improve efficiency, accuracy, and accessibility of school dental services. It will include key features such as a centralized dashboard, appointment scheduling management, patient record management, treatment and routine preventive care (RPC) monitoring, treatment recommendation, predictive-based risk classification, report generation, and an audit trail. These features aim to streamline clinic operations, reduce manual errors, and support better decision-making in delivering oral healthcare services for the school dental clinic.

## **Statement of the Objectives**

**General Objective**  
	To design, develop, and evaluate Floral, a Dental Health Record Management System that centralizes student dental and treatment records across schools, enhances appointment management, and supports data-driven decision-making through automated reporting in Barangay Tanyag, Taguig City, with integrated predictive analytics to identify potential dental health risks and facilitate preventive dental care planning among students.  
**Specific Objectives**  
	The present study will seek answers to the following objectives:

1. To develop a system that analyzes and improves the management of student dental health information covering the following: personal details, medical history, dietary habits, social history, dental health conditions, treatment records, dental charts, and appointment data at Barangay Tanyag school dental clinics.0  
2. To design and develop a system that enables appointment scheduling and monitoring, recording and updating of individual patient treatment records, routine preventive care records, audit trails, and centralized storage of student dental records across schools.  
3. To integrate a predictive analytics module to analyze historical dental records, identify potential dental health conditions, provide treatment recommendations, and risk classification interface through risk stratification categorization of dental health data to the dentist as inputs for a decision-support system.  
4. To generate dashboards that provide an overview of student dental health, reports that summarize treatment history and appointment data, and filterable and searchable dental records that allow school clinic staff to monitor progress and manage follow-ups efficiently.  
5. To test and evaluate the system using the ISO 25010, version 2023 standard on software product quality in terms of:  
   5.1.  Functional Suitability  
   5.2.  Performance Efficiency  
   5.3.  Compatibility  
   5.4.  Usability  
   5.5.  Reliability  
   5.6.  Security

## **Conceptual Framework**

**![][image2]**

### **Figure 1.1.** *Conceptual Framework*

The conceptual framework of this study is based on the Input-Process-Output (IPO) Model \[10\] , which systematically represents the flow of data and processes within the proposed Dental Health Record Management System. The framework is designed to centralize student dental records, enhance appointment management, and support data-driven decision-making through automated reporting and predictive analytics, ultimately facilitating preventive dental care planning across the three covered schools in Barangay Tanyag.  
**Input**  
The input component consists of all data required for system operation and analysis. Student information such as name, age, sex, grade level, and section establishes the foundation of each student's profile. The Individual Patient Treatment Record (IPTR) captures comprehensive medical history, dietary habits, social history, dental charting details, and treatment records. Appointment data is systematically recorded to manage schedules, follow-ups, and visit history. Together, these inputs provide the necessary data for the system to process, analyze, and generate meaningful outputs.  
**Process**  
The process component represents the core system operations that transform input data into meaningful outputs. The system begins with secure user authentication, implementing role-based access control for dentists, dental aides, and school administrators. Dental record management centralizes the recording and updating of student records across all covered schools, while appointment scheduling and monitoring manages clinic appointments, tracks visit status, and flags pending follow-ups. Dental charting functionality enables dentists to record tooth-by-tooth conditions using standard dental marking conventions. The Routine Preventive Care (RPC) tracking module monitors the two-visit preventive care process per student \[11\].  
The predictive analytics component applies machine learning to identify dental health risks and support clinical decision-making. Data preparation and cleaning is first performed to remove errors, handle missing values, and standardize data formats, ensuring the reliability of subsequent analysis. The system then performs data aggregation and centralization, combining student records from all three covered schools into a unified database for comprehensive analysis. Data encryption is applied to protect sensitive student health information, ensuring compliance with data privacy regulations.  
The system proceeds to train and test models using machine learning algorithms to identify students' dental health issues. Performance evaluation is conducted using metrics to validate model reliability. Based on the predicted output, the system generates appropriate treatment recommendations as a decision-support tool for dentist review and validation.   
**Output**  
The output component delivers comprehensive results and insights generated by the system to support clinical decision-making and health monitoring. Centralized student dental records are unified, searchable, and filterable across all three schools. Interactive digital dental charts offer a visual, tooth-by-tooth representation of each student's dental health status using standard dental markings. RPC completion records document the two-visit preventive care progress per student, ensuring accountability and continuity of care. Risk classification results label students as High, Medium, or Low risk, allowing for targeted interventions, while treatment plan suggestions provide condition-appropriate recommendations for dentist review and validation. Appointment summaries and follow-up alerts ensure structured scheduling outcomes and timely reminders. Standardized monthly reports aggregate and structure data in alignment with DOH reporting standards, including providing age-bracket and gender-based counts for monitoring and decision-making. The health dashboard provides a visual, school-wide overview of dental health trends, empowering administrators and public health officials with the insights needed to improve dental health outcomes across the community.

**Significance of the Study**  
	The present study may be beneficial to the following:  
	**The Dentists.** From the results of this study, they may experience a significant improvement in the efficiency and accuracy of dental record management through the use of a centralized digital system. The availability of interactive dental charts, automated patient records, and predictive-based treatment prioritization may enable them to make more informed clinical decisions, reduce the time spent on administrative tasks, and focus more on delivering quality dental care to students.  
	**The Dental Aides.** From the results of this study, dental aides may benefit from a more organized and streamlined workflow in supporting the delivery of dental services. The system may reduce the burden of manual recordkeeping and paperwork, allowing them to assist dentists more effectively and ensure that patient information is accurately recorded, updated, and readily accessible when needed.  
	**The Students.** From the results of this study, students may receive more consistent, timely, and equitable dental care. The system's ability to identify and prioritize students with the most urgent dental health needs may help ensure that no case is overlooked, potentially leading to earlier intervention, fewer complications, and improved dental health outcomes over time.  
	**The School Dental Clinics.** From the results of this study, school dental clinics as institutions may benefit from an efficient and standardized approach to managing dental health. The system may improve the overall capacity of school dental clinics to deliver timely dental care, supporting their mandate under the Department of Health's School Dental Health Care Program.  
	**The School Administrators.** From the results of this study, school administrators may benefit from a more structured and efficient approach to managing dental health data within their institutions. Automated report generation and organized record keeping may reduce their administrative workload.  
	**The Barangay Health Center.** From the results of this study, the Barangay Health Center may directly benefit from the use of the developed system since it follows the same dental processes, recordkeeping practices, and reporting requirements as the school dental clinics. The only difference lies in the age group they serve, as barangay health centers cater to infants and adolescents rather than school-age students. With minimal adjustments, the system may be adopted by the Barangay Health Center to improve the efficiency and accuracy of its own dental health services.  
**The City Health Office.** From the results of this study, the Barangay Health Office may gain access to accurate, consolidated, and up-to-date data on the dental health status of students across all three covered schools. This may support more timely and evidence-based decision-making in the allocation of dental resources and the submission of required reports to the city health office.  
**The Community and Public Health.** From the results of this study, the broader community may benefit from an improved model of school-based dental health service delivery at the barangay level. The system may demonstrate that meaningful advancements in preventive care and health data management are achievable even in resource-limited settings, potentially serving as a replicable framework for other barangay-level school dental programs across the Philippines.  
**The Researchers.** This study may provide the researchers with a deeper understanding of the challenges and opportunities involved in developing and implementing a digital health system in a community-based school setting. The process of designing, developing, and evaluating the system may also strengthen their technical competencies and contribute to their growth as researchers in the field of health informatics and software development.  
**The Future Researchers.** Based on the results of this study, future researchers may use the documented design, development process, and evaluation outcomes as a reference for conducting related studies in similar settings. This study may also serve as a foundation for further exploration of predictive analytics in school health programs and the development of more advanced digital health systems that build upon the findings presented in this research.

**Scope and Limitations of the Study**  
**Scope**  
	This study focuses on the design and development of a web-based Dental Health Record Management System with integrated predictive analytics for the school dental clinics of Barangay Tanyag in Taguig City, specifically covering Bagong Tanyag Integrated School, Bagong Tanyag Elementary School Annex A, and South Daang Hari Elementary School Main. The subjects of the study include the students enrolled in these three schools, along with the dentists, dental aides, clinic staff, school administrators, and city health office who interact with the dental clinic. The system will cover the design and development of a role-based access control, appointment scheduling and monitoring, recording and updating of individual patient treatment records, routine preventive care records, audit trail, and centralized storage of student dental records across schools with integration of a predictive analytics module to analyze historical dental records, identify potential dental health conditions, provide treatment recommendations, and risk classification interface through risk stratification categorization of dental health data to the dentist as inputs for a decision-support system. The study will be conducted within the academic year 2025 to 2026 and will encompass the software development process, from requirements analysis and system design to evaluation using the ISO 25010:2023 standard for software product quality.  
**Limitations**  
	The study is limited to a web application and does not extend to mobile application development. The predictive analytics module is intended to function as a clinical decision support tool to assist in clinical decision-making and treatment planning, but does not replace the professional or clinical judgment of the dentist nor increase physical treatment capacity. The system will operate as a standalone platform without integration with national government databases or external health systems, and features such as computer vision-based caries detection, biometric authentication, and tele-dentistry are outside the scope of this study, as these functionalities are not part of the existing workflow and operational processes of the school dental clinics. Furthermore, the accuracy of the predictive module is dependent on the completeness and correctness of historical treatment data encoded into the system, and the system may require further clinical validation before it can be adapted for use in other districts or larger institutional settings.

## **Definition of Terms**

	**Audit Trail.** It refers to an automatic log recorded by the system that tracks all user actions such as additions, edits, and deletions made to student dental records and clinic data.  
	**Dental Caries.** It refers to tooth decay caused by bacterial acid, and is the primary dental health condition being monitored, recorded, and addressed through the proposed system.  
	**Dental Charting.** In this study, it refers to the digital odontogram within the system used by the dentist to record and update the condition of each tooth of a student during a clinic visit.  
	**Dental Health Record Management System.** In this study, it refers to the proposed web-based system that centralizes student dental records, appointment scheduling, treatment tracking, and predictive analytics across the school dental clinics of Barangay Tanyag.  
	**Decision Support System (DSS).** In this study, it refers to the component of the system that presents treatment recommendations generated by the predictive analytics module to the dentist for review and validation before any clinical action is taken.  
	**DMF/dmf Index**. It refers to a standardized dental scoring system that quantifies a patient's history of tooth decay by counting the number of Decayed, Missing, and Filled teeth, where uppercase letters (DMF) are used for permanent dentition and lowercase letters (dmf) are used for primary or deciduous dentition, and is used in this study as a clinical input variable in the predictive analytics module.  
	**DMFT Score.** It refers to the standard measure used to quantify tooth decay in a population by counting a person's Decayed, Missing, and Filled Teeth, used in this study as a reference indicator of student dental health status.  
	**Electronic Dental Records (EDR).** It refers to the digital documentation of a patient's dental health information, used in this study to refer to existing digital dental health record systems whose findings support the development of the proposed system.  
	**ISO 25010:2023.** It refers to the international standard used in this study to evaluate the software quality of the proposed system across characteristics including functional suitability, usability, reliability, security, and performance efficiency.  
	**National Objectives for Health (NOH).** It refers to the DOH's medium-term health agenda that identifies dental health as a priority area and mandates the implementation of school-based dental health programs, providing the policy basis for this study.  
	**Oral Health Risk Classification.** In this study, it refers to the output generated by the predictive analytics module that categorizes each student into one of three risk levels—High, Medium, or Low—based on the analysis of historical dental records and patient health data, serving as the basis for treatment plan suggestions presented to the dentist for validation.  
	**Oral Prophylaxis.** It refers to the professional cleaning of the teeth performed by the school dentist or dental aide to remove plaque, debris, and calculus deposits, and is one of the components recorded under the Routine Preventive Care tracking module of the proposed system.  
	**Predictive Analytics.** In this study, it refers to the use of machine learning algorithms applied to historical student dental records to identify dental health risks, forecast possible dental conditions, and generate treatment recommendations.  
	**Risk Stratification.** In this study, it refers to the process of categorizing students according to their level of dental health risk based on their dental records and health data, enabling the dentist to prioritize care for those most in need.  
	**Role-Based Access Control.** In this study, it refers to the access management mechanism implemented in the proposed system that restricts each user's permissions and visible features based on their assigned role—specifically Dentist, Dental Aide, or School Administrator—ensuring that sensitive student health information is accessible only to authorized personnel.  
	**Routine Preventive Care (RPC).** In this study, it refers to the structured two-visit preventive dental care process administered to students, which includes dental screening, caries risk assessment, dental hygiene instruction, counseling, oral prophylaxis, and fluoride varnish application, in accordance with the School Dental Health Care Program guidelines.  
	**Treatment Recommendation.** In this study, it refers to the suggested dental intervention generated by the predictive analytics module based on a student's identified risk level, which the dentist reviews and validates before it is applied clinically.

# **Chapter 2** **REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE**

This chapter presents a review of related literature and studies relevant to the current study. As oral health remains a public health concern among Filipino school children, most continue to suffer from untreated tooth decay despite existing government programs designed to address it. Studies reviewed in this chapter explore how it can help improve the way school dental clinics manage patient information, schedule appointments, and plan treatments. The review is organized around six key areas: the role of school-based dental services in the Philippines, the policies and regulations that govern school dental health records, the adoption of electronic health records in Philippine health facilities, related local and foreign studies on health and dental record systems, appointment monitoring and preventive care coordination, and the use of predictive analytics to identify dental health risks and support treatment planning. These studies provide the foundation for understanding the problems the proposed system aims to solve and the approaches that guide its design and development.

## **Related Literature**

**The Role of School-Based Dental Services in the Philippines**

The oral health situation in the Philippines reflects a consistent public health burden that has direct implications for the design of school-based dental health systems. The Philippine News Agency \[1\] reported that the national caries prevalence stands at 72%, making dental disease the leading cause of school absenteeism among Filipino children. In response, it established measurable 2028 targets for oral health improvement and mandated that school-based dental screening data be integrated into the national health information system, making digital record-keeping as a policy priority rather than an optional enhancement.  
At the community level, a study by Oliveros-Villarico et al. \[14\] found that 29.2% of toddlers in Caloocan City, averaging 13.3 months of age, already presented with early childhood caries (ECC), a condition referring to dental decay in children under six years old. The study identified feeding practices, frequency of sugar consumption, and visible dental plaque as the primary risk indicators, all of which are variables that benefit from longitudinal tracking. As children enter school already carrying dental disease that began before their first institutional contact, school dental clinics serve as critical intervention points that must be equipped to document and monitor oral health conditions from the earliest possible encounter.  
A study by Lee et al. \[15\] provided direct evidence of the impact of such services; a study at a low-income school in Manila found that children with prior access to a functional school dental clinic had significantly lower rates of untreated caries compared to newly enrolled students, as measured through caries prevalence rates and Decayed, Missing, and Filled Teeth (DMFT) scores. This finding establishes a strong basis for investing in school dental services that are supported by continuous clinical documentation.  
The evidence on preventive interventions further reinforces the importance of consistent record-keeping in school dental programs. A study conducted by Ruff et al. \[16\] in Camiguin, Philippines, tested school-based fluoride interventions involving daily fluoride toothbrushing and weekly fluoride gel application under the DepEd-GIZ Essential Health Care Programme. The results demonstrated a 22% reduction in caries incidence in the daily toothbrushing group and a 40% reduction in the group that received additional weekly fluoride gel, measured through dft and DMFT indices across intervention and control clusters. Despite these significant clinical outcomes, the study identified inconsistent compliance tracking as a key implementation challenge, noting that the absence of reliable documentation tools undermined the sustainability of monitoring. This finding directly supports the case for digital documentation systems in school dental settings, where treatment records, compliance data, and clinical outcomes must be tracked systematically to sustain the impact of preventive programs.

**Philippine Policy and Regulatory Frameworks Governing School Dental Health Records**  
The development of digital dental health record systems in the Philippines operates within a policy and regulatory environment that establishes both the mandate for such systems and the standards they must meet. The Joint Administrative Order No. 2022-0001, issued by the DOH, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), the Department of Education (DepEd), the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), the Legal Education Board (LEB), the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA), and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) \[17\], established the Healthy Settings Framework for learning institutions. The order mandated that dental and oral health services be treated as minimum required components of school health programs and that compliance records be maintained and submitted for DepEd monitoring. This policy framework gives school dental clinics a legal basis for structured documentation and positions the systematic collection of oral health data as a compliance requirement rather than a discretionary practice.  
Moreover, the DOH Administrative Order No. 2023-0015 \[18\] required the digital transformation of health service delivery at all levels and directed community-level clinical data to be integrated into the national health information ecosystem. Under this mandate, school dental clinics are expected to generate standardized and exportable records that contribute to national monitoring and reporting, making the technical design of school dental record systems a matter of national health policy compliance. The DOH-PHIC Joint Administrative Order No. 2021-002 \[19\] reinforced this direction by mandating national health data standards across all licensed health facilities, specifying standardized data formats for clinical documentation, patient identification, and inter-facility referrals. Any school dental record system must operate within this framework to ensure that the data it generates can be shared and used across the broader health system.

**Electronic Health Records (EHRs) Adoption in Philippine Health Facilities**

A comparative assessment of the Philippine health sector against regional peers by Ulep and Casas \[20\] found that the country lagged behind other ASEAN member states in health information system maturity and digital readiness at the community level, attributing the gap to sustained underinvestment in primary and community health facilities. The assessment, which used health outcome indicators, digital readiness indices, and data from WHO and ASEAN health databases, recommended accelerating digital tool deployment in primary and community settings as a high-leverage national priority. This regional context positions the digitization of school dental clinic records not only as a local operational need but also as part of a larger effort to close the Philippines' digital health gap relative to its neighbors.  
Studies focused specifically on electronic health record (EHR) adoption in Philippine health facilities reveal consistent patterns that inform the design of school dental record systems. Salanguit et al. \[21\] conducted a qualitative case study in Navotas City and found that inadequate health information systems and the absence of digital record-keeping tools undermined the continuity of dental and medical care during school closures in the COVID-19 period, with paper records frequently lost or inaccessible when needed. The study revealed the need for digital record systems capable of offline operation in school clinic settings where internet connectivity may be unreliable.  
Furthermore, a study by Elepano et al. \[22\] across Philippine primary care sites evaluated two EHR systems over three years, achieving an average user survey response rate of 56% across the monitoring period. The study found that offline functionality, simple interfaces, and built-in feedback loops were the strongest predictors of sustained EHR adoption.  
A qualitative evaluation by Evio \[23\], conducted through key informant interviews and focus group discussions with health workers across Philippine health facilities, similarly found that data encoding workload and server dependency were the most frequently cited barriers to EHR use, reinforcing the value of offline-capable and administratively light system designs. A mixed-methods study by De Mesa et al. \[24\] further examined EHR user acceptance across urban, rural, and remote primary care sites in the Philippines, identifying infrastructure constraints and the task-shifting of data entry to nurses as significant adoption barriers. The study recommended cross-platform EHR designs accessible from any device regardless of operating system.  
Moreover, the growth of mobile and web-based health technologies in the Philippines has expanded the range of viable delivery models for digital health record systems, with several studies identifying the conditions under which these tools can succeed in resource-constrained and low-connectivity environments. A narrative review by Macariola et al. \[25\] compared telehealth adoption across ASEAN countries and found that the Philippines was among the fastest-growing adopters in the region during 2020 to 2021\. The review identified Progressive Web Applications (PWAs) as an appropriate technology for low-resource health facilities with variable internet connectivity, as they combine the accessibility of web-based systems with the offline functionality typically associated with native mobile applications. This technology assessment is directly applicable to school dental clinics, which often serve communities where internet access is inconsistent and where devices may be shared among staff. The review reinforced that the willingness of Filipino health workers to adopt digital tools is contingent on those tools offering a clear reduction in workload and on the availability of connectivity-resilient designs.  
The regulatory environment governing mobile and web-based health systems in the Philippines has also evolved to support the integration of digital tools into community health service delivery. The DOH-PHIC Joint Administrative Order No. 2021-002 \[19\] established the technical and data format standards within which all EHR systems, including those operating on web or mobile platforms, must function to ensure interoperability across the national health information ecosystem. For school dental record systems delivered through web-based platforms, compliance with these standards ensures that the data generated at the clinic level can be submitted, shared, or referenced by other health system actors without requiring manual re-encoding or format conversion. Combined with the data security requirements under the NPC Circular No. 2023-06 \[26\] and the Data Privacy Act IRR \[27\], which mandate encryption, audit trails, and access control for any system handling student health records, the regulatory framework collectively defines both the technical architecture and the data governance standards that web-based school dental systems must meet to operate legally and securely in the Philippine context.

## **Related Studies**

**Web-Based Health Record Management Systems in Philippine Community Health Settings**

Several local studies in the Philippines have examined the development of web-based health record management systems designed to replace manual documentation practices in community health facilities. These studies highlight how digital systems can improve record management, increase efficiency, and strengthen healthcare service delivery, particularly in barangay health centers and other resource-limited environments. Olipas et al. \[28\] developed MediCord, a web-based health record management system for a municipal health center in Nueva Ecija, created in response to the disruptions caused by COVID-19. pandemic to traditional record-keeping processes. The study found that thorough planning reduced system complexity and helped streamline the development process, while testing confirmed that the system successfully performed its intended functions. The study further recommended that the remaining SDLC stages be completed and that the actual assessment of the system be based on industry-accepted and widely used standards, directly pointing to the need for a more complete and formally evaluated digital health record system. These recommendations are grounded in the system's demonstrated capacity to reduce data redundancy, prevent unauthorized access to medical files, enable secure sharing of medical clearances across communities, and support timely generation of reports for decision-making.  
Similarly, Batoon et al. \[29\] developed the Public Health Record Management System (PHRMS) for the barangay health center of Sto. Rosario, in Paombong, Bulacan, is addressing several challenges associated with manual record keeping, including misplaced patient files, duplicated records, and the absence of inventory monitoring for medicines and vaccines. Using the Agile Software Development methodology, the researchers designed a system with three access roles: super administrator (midwife), administrator (barangay health workers), and patient users. The system included a real-time patient dashboard, automated reporting tools, vaccination monitoring across puroks, and an inventory alert system for expired or low-stock medicines. Patients were also provided with personalized medication calendars and vaccination reminders through their accounts. Evaluation using the ISO/IEC 25010 Software Quality Model produced high scores across multiple categories, including functionality, performance efficiency, usability, reliability, security, and portability. The study concluded that the system could significantly improve the storage, monitoring, and protection of barangay health records while fully replacing manual processes.  
In a clinical setting, May et al. \[30\] developed Recapp, a web-based healthcare record and appointment management system for the Angeles City Primary HIV Care Clinic (Bale Angeleño) in Pampanga. The system was designed to manage sensitive healthcare records while ensuring strong data privacy. Developed using the Design Thinking methodology, the platform utilized technologies such as PHP/Laravel, ReactJS, Node.js, Tailwind CSS, and phpMyAdmin. To strengthen security, the system incorporated SSL certification, data encryption, and file encryption as layered protection measures. Through the system, patients were able to monitor appointments, medications, and laboratory results, while healthcare staff gained access to statistical reports, medication records, and patient histories through a centralized dashboard. User evaluations indicated that the majority of respondents strongly agreed with the system’s usability, and the study concluded that the platform provided “excellent service” and significantly improved the clinic’s previous manual record system. Taken together, these studies demonstrate that web-based health record systems can improve documentation accuracy, strengthen data security, and enhance healthcare service delivery in Philippine community health facilities.

**Evaluation of Electronic Dental Records (EDRs) in Design, Adoption, and Usability in the Philippines**  
Local studies on dental record digitization have explored both the development of electronic dental record (EDR) systems and the experiences of dentists in adopting these technologies. These studies provide valuable insights into the key features required for effective EDR systems and the practical considerations involved in their implementation. As such, Arbas-Samar and San Antonio \[31\] developed a new Electronic Dental Record (EDR) system for private dental clinics in Laguna, involving 32 dentists and 3 IT experts in identifying the limitations of traditional paper-based records. Dentists highlighted several key requirements for the system, including strong data security, cross-device accessibility, efficient search functionality, comprehensive patient data storage, and user-friendly design. After development, the system was evaluated by both groups. Dentists rated the system as acceptable and particularly appreciated the restricted access controls and step-by-step user tutorial. Meanwhile, IT experts evaluated the system as very good across several quality dimensions, including functionality, usability, efficiency, portability, reliability, and maintainability. The researchers concluded that secure data management is the most critical requirement for electronic dental record systems and recommended that future system development remain responsive to the evolving needs of dental practitioners.  
Moreover, Mendoza et al. \[32\] investigated dentists’ attitudes toward the adoption of electronic dental records through a qualitative study using a descriptive design. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis with QSR NVIVO software. The results indicated that dentists perceived several benefits of EDR systems, including improved treatment planning, faster retrieval of patient records, and more reliable payment tracking. Respondents also reported that EDR systems were cost-effective in the long term, as reduced paper usage and improved documentation processes enhanced overall clinic efficiency. However, several challenges were also identified, including concerns about system reliability, dependence on stable internet connectivity, and initial implementation costs. The study concluded that EDR systems are effective tools for managing patient records and supporting clinical decision-making, and most participants recommended their adoption in dental practice.  
In an academic institutional setting, Lacasandile et al. \[33\] developed NU-DREAM (National University Dental Records Electronic Access Management) for the National University-MOA College of Dentistry. The system was designed to support the clinical training of fifth and sixth-year dentistry students by digitizing patient charts, clinic logs, tally sheets, and clinical training documentation. The researchers used a prototyping approach and conducted focus group discussions with end users to refine system requirements and interface design. Through the platform, clinical instructors and administrators were able to monitor student performance using daily digital clinical reports. The study concluded that the system helped modernize clinical documentation processes within the university clinic and improved the monitoring of student training activities. Collectively, these studies indicate that while electronic dental records are generally well received in dental practice, successful implementation depends on addressing concerns related to security, usability, and system reliability.  
Similarly situated in an academic context, Hernández-Cruz et al. \[34\] developed a digital dental clinical record system for a higher education institution using the Rapid Application Development (RAD) methodology, which consists of four phases: requirements, design, production and testing, and implementation. The system was designed as an information system, with the primary goal of supporting the follow-up of academic dental practices during the development of both generic and specific competencies in dentistry programs. The study reported that the implemented system directly improved the efficiency and effectiveness of dental clinical record management, reducing both record capture time and human errors while enhancing the overall quality of patient care. The researchers highlighted that the interactive interface and ease of use were the system's most significant contributors to its operational success and concluded that software management can function as a strategic tool for optimizing patient care in academic dental settings.

**Integrated Dental Health Record Management Systems in the Philippines**  
Beyond basic record storage, several local studies have explored more comprehensive dental clinic management systems that integrate multiple operational functions within a single platform. A project was developed called Mabida DCMS \[35\], a dental clinic management system that integrates several clinic operations into a unified digital platform. The system includes patient registration, appointment scheduling with automated email and SMS reminders, treatment planning with diagnostic image integration, electronic billing with insurance processing, inventory monitoring with low-stock alerts, and staff management functions. Role-based access control was implemented to protect sensitive patient information, while the responsive system design allowed access across different devices. The study highlighted that integrating these functions within a single platform improves workflow efficiency, reduces scheduling conflicts, minimizes billing errors, and supports more informed clinical decision-making through easy access to patient treatment histories.  
Furthermore, Elicanal et al. \[36\]  developed Wisdom Dental, a digital booking and e-commerce platform designed for Wisdom Dental Clinic in Pasig City. The system integrated online appointment scheduling, dental product purchasing, teleconsultation services, and automated report generation. Additionally, the platform incorporated predictive analytics using the Exponential Smoothing algorithm for time-series forecasting. Developed using the Waterfall SDLC model and technologies such as PHP, MySQL, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, the system was evaluated using ISO 25010 standards by 50 respondents, including both users and technical evaluators. The results indicated high satisfaction ratings, suggesting that the system successfully improved service delivery and operational efficiency. Additional features, including a first-come-first-serve scheduling algorithm and a downpayment mechanism, were implemented to reduce appointment no-shows, while the predictive analytics module generated seven-day income forecasts to support administrative planning.  
In an institutional context, Buctuan and Cagas \[37\] developed an Agile-driven digital health and dental record management system for Surigao del Norte State University. The system incorporated six modules: Student, Employee, Health, Dental, Medical Supplies, and E-log. Using the Agile Scrum methodology, the platform was developed iteratively through continuous stakeholder feedback. Evaluation using ISO/IEC 25010 standards demonstrated strong usability, reliability, and adaptability of the system. The study concluded that the platform provides a scalable model for digital transformation in academic healthcare record management. Taken together, these studies show that dental clinic management systems in the Philippines are gradually evolving from simple record digitization tools into integrated platforms capable of supporting scheduling automation and integration of predictive analytics.  
A further development was presented by Caluban et al. \[38\], who designed a web-based Dental Information Management System with SMS notifications and a Decision Support System (DSS) for Idagdag Tooth Care Clinic in Panabo City, Davao del Norte. The system was developed using the Waterfall Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) model. One of its main features is a DSS that uses the K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) algorithm to help dentists identify possible tooth diseases. This feature allows dentists to upload patient photographs to the system, which are then analyzed by the algorithm to support diagnosis. In addition, the system includes SMS notifications that automatically send appointment reminders to patients, helping reduce missed visits. To evaluate the system, the researchers used the User Experience Questionnaire (UEQ) with 25 sample users. The results showed positive scores across all quality dimensions, including attractiveness (2.01), pragmatic quality (1.96), and hedonic quality (1.79), all of which are higher than the positive evaluation threshold of 0.08. The clinic sponsor also expressed support for implementing the system. The researchers recommended several future improvements, such as adding dental charting, payroll automation, and inventory monitoring modules. The study shows that decision-support algorithms and automated patient communication can be successfully integrated into dental record management systems.  
Building on this integration of decision support into clinic workflows, Ramos et al. \[39\] developed a Dental Clinic Appointment Management System with Decision Support designed to address challenges in scheduling, patient record management, and communication within a dental clinic setting. The study employed a descriptive research design, collecting both qualitative and quantitative data through interviews, surveys, and observations involving dentists, clinic staff, and patients. The developed system resolved common problems associated with manual scheduling, including appointment conflicts, missed visits, and service delays. Its core features include real-time appointment booking, automated reminders, centralized patient record management, and a decision support module that prioritizes appointments based on urgency and availability. Profile avatars for patients and dentists were also incorporated to enhance user identification and interface personalization. Evaluation by IT experts indicated that the system achieved a "Very Great Extent" of compliance with ISO/IEC 25010 software quality standards across functionality, usability, reliability, maintainability, and efficiency, demonstrating that appointment management systems with embedded clinical prioritization logic can significantly streamline dental clinic operations.  
Overall, these studies show that dental clinic management systems in the Philippines have gradually evolved from simple digital record systems into more integrated platforms that support scheduling automation, predictive analytics, and decision-support tools. These related studies provide a strong foundation for the system proposed in the present study.

**Appointment Monitoring and Preventive Care Coordination in Dental Health Services**  
Markose \[41\] examined the application of predictive analytics to identify high-risk patients within the Medicare population and reduce adverse health events through targeted preventive care. The study applied random forest and neural network models to electronic health records and digital health databases, with the random forest model achieving an AUC-ROC of 0.85 and the neural network reaching 0.82. Care coordination plans and early warning systems derived from model outputs contributed to a 20% decrease in heart failure readmissions and a 15% reduction in diabetes incidence among the targeted population. While this study addresses a general healthcare context, its framework for integrating predictive risk models into patient record systems and appointment workflows has direct relevance to dental health systems that manage patients with complex medical histories and require automated mechanisms for prioritizing preventive care scheduling.  
In a dentistry-specific context, Alabdulkarim et al. \[42\] developed predictive models for dental appointment no-shows using a dataset of 262,140 appointment records from a dental clinic in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Three algorithms were evaluated, logistic regression, random forests, and gradient boosting, with gradient boosting achieving the best performance at an AUC of 0.718 and an F1-score of 66.5%. The most influential predictors of non-attendance were appointment lead time, appointment month, and day of the week. The models were designed to support overbooking decisions and optimize resource allocation, showing that appointment history data maintained within a dental management system can be directly leveraged for scheduling analytics. The study confirms that structured appointment records, when systematically stored, provide sufficient information to forecast attendance behavior and reduce the operational impact of missed appointments.  
Moreover, Weber et al. \[43\] used business intelligence tools and logistic regression to analyze over 410,000 appointment records from the University of Michigan Dental School clinics, identifying factors associated with failed dental appointments. Prior attendance history was found to be the strongest predictor of future attendance. Patients who reported dental anxiety were 62% as likely to attend their appointments compared to those without such concerns. The communication method also significantly influenced attendance: patients who received SMS text reminders were 1.22 times more likely to attend than those who received phone calls, while those emailed a reminder achieved a 94.9% attendance rate and text-reminded patients achieved 92.2%. The study demonstrates that appointment and patient communication records stored in a dental management system can be analyzed to develop evidence-based scheduling strategies and patient outreach protocols that reduce non-attendance rates.  
Complementing the findings on scheduling behavior, Simmons et al. \[44\] used electronic dental health records to identify and manage high-risk caries patients within a dataset of 86,025 individuals at a dental safety-net clinic. Patients flagged as high risk through EDR-based risk stratification were paired with a dental care advocate (DCA), a trained staff member responsible for facilitating appointment scheduling, attendance, and care coordination. The intervention produced significant increases in the odds of scheduling an appointment. The study demonstrates that combining structured patient risk data from electronic dental records with targeted human support substantially improves patient engagement in care. This finding is applicable to dental health record systems that incorporate patient monitoring and care coordination workflows, where patient data drives both automated alerts and personalized follow-up actions.

**Application of Predictive Analytics for Identification of Dental Health Condition**  
Swinckels et al. \[45\] developed a machine learning model using non-image electronic dental records (EDRs) to predict periodontal disease (PD) risk, a chronic inflammatory condition affecting the gums and supporting structures of the teeth. The study drew structured data from 43,331 participants stored in the BigMouth repository, a large collaborative dental data platform. A Random Forest model, which constructs multiple decision trees and aggregates their outputs for more stable and accurate predictions, achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 94% and a sensitivity of 81%, with validation sensitivity reaching 91%. These results indicate that the model correctly identified high-risk individuals in most cases. The study supports the value of integrating automated risk stratification into electronic dental record systems, where structured patient data can be analyzed to flag individuals who require early preventive care before clinical deterioration occurs.  
In a related effort to predict oral disease, Bomfim \[46\] applied machine learning to predict untreated dental caries among 615 adolescents using data from an epidemiological survey conducted in Brazil. Several algorithms were compared, and XGBoost, a gradient-boosted decision tree algorithm that builds models sequentially to correct the errors of previous iterations — outperformed others with an area under the curve (AUC) of 84%, compared to 81% for the decision tree model. The most influential predictors identified were dental floss use, consumption of unhealthy foods, self-declared race, and exposure to fluoridated water. This finding demonstrates that structured sociodemographic and behavioral data, the type routinely collected during patient intake in dental health records, can be effectively used to identify adolescents at risk of caries before clinical signs are fully evident, enabling targeted preventive interventions.  
In addition, Salahov et al. \[47\] developed a digital predictive technology using discriminant analysis, a statistical classification method that assigns observations to groups based on a set of measured variables, to forecast caries development in individual teeth. The model was built using questionnaire responses from 200 patients and achieved classification accuracies of 50.0–92.6% for upper teeth and 50.4–77.3% for lower teeth, with higher accuracy for teeth exhibiting more distinct risk patterns. A notable strength of the study is its capacity to forecast caries risk up to two years in advance, enabling timely preventive action before disease progression. The findings highlight the potential of patient-reported data, including dietary habits and oral hygiene practices, as predictive inputs within a structured dental health record system capable of generating individualized risk forecasts.  
Shifting focus to periodontal disease, Patel et al. \[48\] developed a periodontal disease prediction model using the XGBoost algorithm and EDR data from 27,138 patients at Temple University Kornberg School of Dentistry. A total of 74 features were extracted from the records, encompassing patient-level variables such as anxiety, teeth grinding, alcohol consumption, medication use, and systemic conditions including cardiovascular disease and diabetes. The model was trained on 80% of the data using a five-fold cross-validation strategy and achieved an AUC of 0.72 in distinguishing healthy patients from mild and severe PD cases. The study revealed the importance of maintaining detailed medical and social history fields in dental records, as such data meaningfully enhances the predictive power of machine learning models applied to periodontal risk assessment.  
In a similar investigation targeting caries risk in younger populations, Kang et al. \[49\] developed the Dental Caries Prediction (DCP) model using data from the 2018 Korean children’s oral health survey administered by the Korean Center for Disease Control and Prevention, encompassing 22,287 samples. Among six tested algorithms, including SVM, gradient-boosted decision trees, logistic regression, artificial neural networks, and convolutional neural networks, Random Forest achieved the highest performance with 92% accuracy, an F1-score of 90%, precision of 94%, and recall of 87%. The study demonstrated that structured survey data containing demographic, regional, and behavioral variables could train a robust and practically applicable caries risk model. These results confirm the utility of systematic oral health survey data as the basis for automated prediction within dental health management systems that require early risk identification.  
Moving beyond clinical variables, Hung et al. \[50\] examined the relationship between social determinants of health and unmet dental care needs using data from the 2016 Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS), which contained 237 selected predictors drawn from 1,941 variables. A decision tree classifier, which sorts patient data through a hierarchical series of conditional rules to reach a classification outcome, and a deep learning neural network with three hidden layers were used and compared. The deep learning model outperformed the decision tree, achieving an accuracy of 82.6%, sensitivity of 77.8%, specificity of 87.4%, precision of 82.9%, and an AUC of 0.918. The study established that social history variables, including income level, insurance coverage, and geographical access to dental services, are among the strongest predictors of unmet oral health needs. This finding emphasizes the importance of recording social history alongside clinical data in patient records to enable population-level risk analytics within dental health information systems.

**Enhancement of Treatment Planning through Decision Support Systems**  
Parkhi et al. \[51\] developed a deep learning classification framework for oral diseases using 10,573 clinically sourced dental data points processed through a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). The model achieved a mean classification accuracy of 87.6%, with a training accuracy of 86.69% and a validation accuracy of 87.61%. A confidence thresholding mechanism was incorporated into the framework to identify ambiguous cases that require clinician review, which improves the practical reliability of automated decisions in a clinical setting. The framework supports the development of diagnostic assistance tools within dental health systems, where automated preliminary assessment based on stored patient data can augment dentist evaluation and ensure that clinical determinations and their supporting evidence are consistently documented in patient records.  
In a complementary approach that embedded decision support directly into clinical workflows, Mullins et al. \[52\] evaluated the effect of an electronic health record-based clinical decision support system (CDSS), a tool that generates real-time clinical guidance based on patient record data, on the appropriate placement of dental sealants in a high-risk pediatric population. The study analyzed 59,047 examination visits spanning January 2018 to December 2022\. Following CDSS implementation in September 2020, the rate of appropriate sealant placement at examination visits increased from 27% to 60% (p \< .00001). The results provide direct evidence that embedding structured decision support within an EHR system significantly improves clinical adherence to evidence-based preventive guidelines. This finding is applicable to web-based dental health record systems that can incorporate patient-driven recommendation modules linked to examination outcomes and treatment records.  
Ameli et al. \[53\] further explored the use of multiple machine learning techniques to automate the review of patient chart information from 785 anonymized dental clinic records. Text mining and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), an algorithm that groups semantically related content from large text datasets into distinct topics, were applied to preprocess unstructured clinical notes and extract 10 radiographic finding topics and 8 treatment planning topics. Ordinal Logistic Regression (OLR) and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) were then used to identify predictive relationships between these extracted topics and oral health outcomes such as caries risk, periodontitis, gingival recession, and bruxism. The ANN model correctly predicted more than 72% of outcomes for 8 of the 10 variables assessed. The study shows that even unstructured clinical notes stored within patient record systems can be processed into structured predictive inputs, reinforcing the analytic value of comprehensive charting and documentation practices in dental records.

## **Relevance of Related Literature and Studies to the Current Study**

	The reviewed literature and studies present significant developments in dental health systems, particularly in the use of electronic dental records, machine learning, and digital management platforms. Several studies show that predictive analytics can improve decision-making in dental care, and that shifting from manual to digital record systems leads to better efficiency, data accessibility, and clinical performance. Most of these systems are designed for specialized clinical environments and address only specific aspects of dental care, leaving a need for a more comprehensive and integrated solution suited to school-based settings.  
The reviewed studies reveal that existing systems tend to address only one specific operational concern, such as appointment scheduling, disease prediction, treatment planning, or record digitization, without integrating these functions into one complete platform. None of the reviewed systems integrate patient record management, dental health and dental charting, appointment scheduling, predictive analytics for treatment recommendations, and report generation within a single, accessible solution, particularly in a school-based or local clinical setting.  
This gap guides the development of the present study, which proposes a web-based dental health record management system with predictive analytics designed specifically for school clinics. Unlike the systems reviewed, the proposed system integrates every core function of dental health management, from patient and dental health records to appointments, treatments, clinical decision support, and report generation, into one unified and accessible platform. The studies presented in this chapter served as a guide in identifying these unmet needs, and the concepts, approaches, and findings drawn from the reviewed literature informed the design decisions, feature selection, and functional scope of the system that the succeeding chapters will discuss in detail.
